nodes.name: Midnight sun & polar night
nodes.desc: Plants and algae can only grow in the bright summer months, when the sun stays above the horizon for weeks; in winter the long polar night shuts growth down.

nodes.name: Sea ice
nodes.desc: Frozen sea surface that carries a bloom of algae, serves as a hunting platform for polar bears and a breeding platform for ringed seals.

nodes.name: Snow cover & ice crusts
nodes.desc: Snow shelters tundra plants through winter and melts into summer water. Rain falling on snow can freeze into an ice crust that locks reindeer out of their food.

nodes.name: Thin tundra soil & bird guano
nodes.desc: Soils are thin and thaw only in summer. Seabird droppings below bird cliffs fertilise the slopes, where the lushest vegetation grows.

nodes.name: Soil microbes & fungi
nodes.desc: Break down dead plants, carcasses and droppings slowly in the cold, returning nutrients to the thin soil.

nodes.name: Phytoplankton
nodes.desc: Drifting microscopic algae that bloom in spring and summer in fjords and along the ice edge. They feed copepods and sink to feed the seabed.

nodes.name: Polar willow
nodes.desc: A tiny creeping willow of Arctic tundra, a few centimetres tall. Reindeer and rock ptarmigan eat it.

nodes.name: Alpine bistort
nodes.desc: A small tundra herb whose leaves and bulbils are eaten by birds such as the rock ptarmigan.

nodes.name: Tundra grass
nodes.desc: A grass of wet Arctic tundra, one of the grasses and sedges that grazing reindeer and geese use in summer.

nodes.name: Arctic copepods
nodes.desc: Tiny, fat-rich crustaceans that graze the spring algae bloom and pass that energy to fish and seabirds.

nodes.name: Clams & seafloor bivalves
nodes.desc: Bottom-dwelling bivalves that filter food from the water and from sinking algae. They are a main food of walruses.

nodes.name: Svalbard reindeer
nodes.desc: A small, sedentary reindeer that grazes tundra plants all year. Nearly wiped out by hunting, it has recovered, but ice-sealed winter pastures can cause die-offs.

nodes.name: Barnacle goose
nodes.desc: Breeds in Svalbard and winters on the Solway Firth. Goslings leap from cliff nests and often fall to Arctic foxes.

nodes.name: Rock ptarmigan
nodes.desc: The only bird that stays in Svalbard through winter, living on buds, twigs and seeds of low tundra plants.

nodes.name: Arctic cod
nodes.desc: A small, abundant fish of cold water that eats copepods and is a key food for seals and seabirds.

nodes.name: Arctic char
nodes.desc: A cold-water fish found in Svalbard lakes and rivers, with sea-going and lake-bound populations. It takes insects, crustaceans and small fish, and polar bears eat it.

nodes.name: Little auk
nodes.desc: A sparrow-sized seabird nesting in huge scree-slope colonies, feeding chiefly on copepods. Its colonies are raided by Arctic foxes and glaucous gulls.

nodes.name: Ringed seal
nodes.desc: Lives in and under sea ice, keeping breathing holes open and giving birth in snow lairs. It is the polar bear's main prey.

nodes.name: Walrus
nodes.desc: Digs clams from the seabed with its whiskers and snout. Hunted almost out of Svalbard by 1952, it has since recovered under protection.

nodes.name: Glaucous gull
nodes.desc: A large gull that preys on seabird chicks and eggs, such as those of little auks, and takes seal pups and scraps.

nodes.name: Arctic fox
nodes.desc: Hunts and scavenges across tundra and shore, taking eggs, birds, reindeer and seal pups, including the leftovers of polar bear kills.

nodes.name: Polar bear
nodes.desc: Svalbard's top predator, hunting ringed seals from the sea ice. It also takes reindeer, geese, eggs and walrus calves when seals are scarce.
